title: Get started
text: CouchDB-inspired views · Rust · Python · browser Write a view once. Run it anywhere. Map documents into live views with portable AssemblyScript and WebAssembly. Run the same compiled view in a native Rust database or entirely in a browser worker. Try it in your browser ↗ Build a portable view 01 Append Any finite JSON value → 02 Map Emit a key and contribution → 03 Reduce Read the current group state Unreleased development API. This portable API has not been released on PyPI. These instructions describe the local checkout; remote source and the hosted site can lag changes until publication. Use a checkout containing native/ and views/ , or a wheel built from that checkout. Install from your checkout Build prerequisites are Python 3.11+, Rust/Cargo 1.90+, and a platform C compiler and linker. SQLite is bundled with the extension. Run from the repository root: python -m venv .venv . .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip python -m pip install . python examples/portable_metrics.py On Windows, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate in an MSVC build environment. No Node compiler is needed for the bundled views. To build a local wheel, run python -m pip wheel . --no-deps --wheel-dir dist , then install the resulting .whl on a matching platform. Installing a built wheel needs neither Rust nor Node. PyPI release setup remains pending. A native metric in a few lines The bundled metrics module maps each payload's string metric and numeric value , maintaining count, sum, minimum, maximum, and mean. Start with a fresh metrics.db file: from foldlitedb import PortableDatabase, PortableView metrics = PortableView.bundled("metrics") with PortableDatabase("metrics.db", metrics) as db: documents = db.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result == { "count": 2, "sum": 12, "min": 4, "max": 8, "mean": 6, } Rust executes both map and reduce through a bounded Wasm interpreter and commits the resulting view in SQLite. There are no Python callbacks on this path. add_many returns resolved documents, including generated IDs and source positions. Retain those records outside the derived database for replay. Append freely. Name when useful. Each unnamed add(payload) creates a new observation. Supply a source-scoped name when identical retries should count once. Documents are immutable; conflicting reuse raises DocumentConflict . with PortableDatabase("metrics.db", metrics) as db: saved = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}, id="measurement-3") assert db.add(saved.payload, id="measurement-3") == saved documents += (saved,) External logs can supply source and monotonically increasing position instead. Resolved Document records replay through ingest without counting twice. Read once, follow changes rows() follows bounded snapshot pages. Use query() when you also need a cursor for subsequent changes: with PortableDatabase("metrics.db", metrics) as db: snapshot = db.query() fourth = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 1}) updates = db.changes(since=snapshot.cursor) assert updates.rows[0].result["mean"] == 4 retained = tuple(db.documents()) with PortableDatabase("rebuilt.db", metrics) as rebuilt: rebuilt.ingest(retained) assert list(rebuilt.rows())[0].result["mean"] == 4 Each batch commits documents, checkpoints, group states, and changes together. The native engine currently holds one exact module per database. A different module needs a fresh database and replay. The same module, entirely in a browser Open the static playground , import JSON or JSONL, and watch groups update locally. Its dedicated worker executes the same compiled module used by Python. Export documents and verify a replay before closing the page: browser storage is currently in memory. The browser integration example includes the exact client import, resource-copy step, and a working static page. No application server is needed to process documents. Using Python callbacks instead The existing Database API supports trusted Python maps, ordered folds, and multiple views in a separate SQLite schema. Install python -m pip install '.[reducers]' for its numeric Rust/Wasm reducers, or use dependency-free Python OrderedFold . Source installation still builds the native extension and requires Rust. Callback maps and folds run in Python; they do not become browser view modules. See the callback API and examples for registration, named-view reads, automatic rebuilds, and compaction. Keep exploring Write a portable view ↗ A complete AssemblyScript module, custom build, and browser integration. The native Python API ↗ Appends, replay, snapshots, changes, export, and lifecycle. Replay and ordering ↗ Document identity, module versions, persistence, and numerical limits. Earlier native experiments ↗ Historical numeric field-map measurements with their original scope.

text: The same view. A new place to run it. Your browser. Your live database. CouchDB-inspired map/reduce, running right here. An AssemblyScript view maps your documents and reduces each group in WebAssembly. No server required. Local workspace Starting WebAssembly worker… 0 retained documents 0 live groups 0 committed sequence Ready replay verification 01 Bring your documents Drop a JSON or JSONL file A document array, or one document per line. Choose a file ↗ Up to 1,024 small documents per import. Files stay in this browser. Add a measurement Metric Value Add + Paste JSON or JSONL Raw documents Import documents 02 Watch your views update metrics@1 map → group → reduce Start live stream Live metrics computed by the WebAssembly view Metric Count Mean Min Max Loading the example… Observed range min — ● — max · dot = mean ↻ Rebuild & verify Export documents ↓ Reset example Loading the shared view module. ✓ AssemblyScript → WebAssembly → dedicated worker Inspect the module View Loading… SHA-256, verified before execution Loading… Storage In memory. Export documents before reloading this page. Isolation No host imports. Maximum 16 MiB of WebAssembly memory. Worker requests have a deadline. JavaScript retains documents and groups emitted keys. The AssemblyScript module performs every map and reduction. This is the same compiled artifact used by the native engine. Enable JavaScript to run this local map/reduce example. Write a view once. Run it here or in Python. The metrics module accepts documents with a string metric and a finite numeric value . Its map emits the metric as a key. Its reducer maintains count, sum, minimum, and maximum; finalization computes the mean. Other document shapes are ignored by the map. Numbers use double precision in both environments. Keep large identifiers as strings. Strings must be valid Unicode; each module request is limited to 256 KiB of encoded JSON. Browser · no backend import { BrowserDatabase } from "./portable/client.js"; const db = await BrowserDatabase.connect(); await db.add({ metric: "latency_ms", value: 42 }); const rows = await db.rows(); console.log(rows[0].result); db.close(); Python · the same metrics.wasm from foldlitedb import PortableDatabase, PortableView view = PortableView.bundled("metrics") with PortableDatabase("metrics.db", view) as db: db.add({"metric": "latency_ms", "value": 42}) row = list(db.rows())[0] print(row.result) Your documents are the source of truth Try the live stream, add a few measurements, then select Rebuild & verify . A fresh in-memory database replays every retained document through the same module and compares its complete view states and results. Existing views keep their cursors. Exported JSON includes document identities, sources, positions, and payloads. Importing it again is an identical replay: each retained document counts once. Changing an existing identity or position fails the whole batch. Use those same records to rebuild the native database. A portable computation preview. This browser database keeps documents and view history in memory. Export them to keep your work. The live stream is simulated locally; this page makes no requests containing your documents. Python provides the persistent Rust-backed engine.

title: Portable views
text:
CouchDB-inspired views, from Python to the browser Write a view once. Run it in either environment. A portable view contains both its map and its reducer. AssemblyScript compiles them into one WebAssembly module, executed by the Rust engine or a browser worker. Try the browser playground Write a custom view Development API. This portable API has not been released on PyPI. Build this checkout or install a wheel built from it. The native engine currently holds one view per database; the browser host keeps state in memory. The existing callback Database API remains available separately. A native database from Python Build prerequisites are Python 3.11+, Rust/Cargo 1.90+, and a platform C compiler and linker. From the repository root: python -m pip install . python examples/portable_metrics.py SQLite and the precompiled modules are included. Node is needed only for authoring or rebuilding AssemblyScript. To produce a wheel locally, run python -m pip wheel . --no-deps --wheel-dir dist . Installing the resulting wheel on a matching platform needs no compiler. See environment setup for virtual-environment and Windows notes. Start the following example with fresh database files: from foldlitedb import PortableDatabase, PortableView view = PortableView.bundled("metrics") with PortableDatabase("portable-metrics.db", view) as db: documents = db.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result["mean"] == 6 snapshot = db.query() db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}) assert db.changes(since=snapshot.cursor).rows[0].result["mean"] == 5 retained = tuple(db.documents()) Rust owns document identity, SQLite transactions, checkpoints, group states, snapshots, and changes. Its bounded Wasm interpreter executes both mapping and reduction, with no Python callbacks or Python Wasmtime dependency. rows() follows paginated snapshots; explicit query() and changes() support resumable reads. The Python reference covers every portable method. Two bundled views Metrics accepts payloads with a string metric and finite numeric value . Valid documents emit one number under their metric key; malformed shapes, missing fields, nulls, and nonnumeric values emit nothing. States contain {count,sum,min,max} ; finalized results add mean . Empty states use null minimum, maximum, and mean. This view supports merge. Invalid contributions, states, and numeric overflow fail. Catalogue accepts {category:string,id:string,title:string,deleted?:boolean} . Each category folds item IDs to their latest titles. An event with {category,id,deleted:true} removes that item. Finalization returns {count,items:{id:title}} . Event order matters, so this view does not support merge. Malformed documents emit nothing; item IDs are limited to 65,535 UTF-16 code units. Author a complete view Use Node.js 20+ and the pinned SDK dependencies. The bundled build handles exactly metrics and catalogue ; it does not discover additional files: npm ci --prefix views npm run build --prefix views npm test --prefix views npm run check --prefix views For a custom module, save this complete source as views/assembly/examples/metric-totals.ts . It groups numeric values by metric and returns a running total. The SDK handles UTF-8 buffers, finite JSON, allocation, dispatch, and error envelopes. import { JSON, View, Emission, object, numeric, number, dispatch } from "../sdk"; export { abi_version, input_ptr, input_capacity, output_ptr } from "../sdk"; class MetricTotals extends View { constructor() { super("metric-totals", false, "1", "1"); } map(document: JSON.Value): Emission[] { const doc = object(document); if (doc == null) return []; const metric = doc.get("metric"); const value = doc.get("value"); if (metric == null || metric.type != JSON.Types.String || !numeric(value)) { return []; } return [new Emission(metric, value!)]; } identity(): JSON.Value { return JSON.Value.from(0); } add(state: JSON.Value, values: JSON.Arr): JSON.Value { if (!numeric(state)) return this.fail("Invalid total state"); let total = number(state); for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) { const value = values.at(i); if (!numeric(value)) return this.fail("Expected a numeric contribution"); total += number(value); } if (!isFinite(total)) return this.fail("Total overflowed"); return JSON.Value.from(total); } finalize(state: JSON.Value): JSON.Value { if (!numeric(state)) return this.fail("Invalid total state"); return state; } } const view = new MetricTotals(); export function execute(length: i32): i32 { return dispatch(view, length); } Compile from views/ using the same compiler settings as the bundled modules. These are POSIX-shell commands: cd views mkdir -p .build JSON_MODE=naive node node_modules/assemblyscript/bin/asc.js \ assembly/examples/metric-totals.ts \ --outFile .build/metric-totals.wasm \ --transform json-as --runtime incremental \ --maximumMemory 256 --initialMemory 16 --stackSize 32768 \ --use abort=assembly/sdk/index/abort \ --optimizeLevel 3 --shrinkLevel 1 While still in views/ , generate the digest manifest used by the browser. The descriptor is read from the compiled module, so it matches the view name, version, state version, and merge capability: node --input-type=module <<'JS' import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises'; import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'; const bytes = await readFile('.build/metric-totals.wasm'); const module = new WebAssembly.Module(bytes); if (WebAssembly.Module.imports(module).length) throw new Error('Unexpected imports'); const { exports: api } = new WebAssembly.Instance(module); const input = new TextEncoder().encode('{"op":"descriptor"}'); new Uint8Array(api.memory.buffer).set(input, api.input_ptr()); const length = api.execute(input.length); const response = JSON.parse(new TextDecoder().decode( new Uint8Array(api.memory.buffer, api.output_ptr(), length))); if (!response.ok) throw new Error(response.error); const manifest = { abi: 1, module: 'metric-totals.wasm', sha256: createHash('sha256').update(bytes).digest('hex'), descriptor: response.ok, }; await writeFile('.build/metric-totals.json', JSON.stringify(manifest, null, 2) + '\n'); JS cd .. Back at the repository root, load the same bytes from Python. This example follows the custom compilation steps above: import json from pathlib import Path from foldlitedb import PortableDatabase, PortableView manifest = json.loads(Path("views/.build/metric-totals.json").read_text()) custom = PortableView("views/.build/metric-totals.wasm", sha256=manifest["sha256"]) with PortableDatabase(":memory:", custom) as db: db.add_many([{"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result == 12 The map receives payloads only, not host IDs or positions. Include domain metadata inside the payload if your computation needs it. Keys, states, and contributions can be structured JSON. State is passed explicitly to every update; requests must not depend on mutable module globals, clocks, randomness, or undeclared external data. Hosts instantiate the module afresh for operations. add must preserve contribution order and produce equivalent state when an input sequence is split into successive batches. Implement merge and set mergeable=true only when compatible independent states can be combined correctly. The example leaves merge disabled. Bump the view version for changed behavior and the state version for incompatible formats; rebuild the module and manifest together. A new compiler can also change the module digest. Use the module on a static website The playground imports JSON arrays or JSONL, appends measurements, streams simulated updates, exports resolved records, and verifies replay. All document processing stays in its worker. The same module bytes power the Python example; JavaScript owns browser grouping and storage. The Rust SQLite engine itself is not part of the browser build. To create your own page, copy the installed package's browser files and bundled modules. Run this Python from the repository root: from pathlib import Path from foldlitedb import portable_assets target = Path("browser-demo/portable") target.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) for resource in portable_assets().iterdir(): if resource.is_file(): (target / resource.name).write_bytes(resource.read_bytes()) Save this as browser-demo/index.html . Browser methods are asynchronous; addMany returns a batch-result object, while Python's add_many returns a tuple of documents. Foldlite DB in the browser 
Loading…
python -m http.server 8000 --directory browser-demo Open http://localhost:8000 ; opening the file directly is insufficient for module workers and fetch. Production deployments can serve these files over HTTPS. Keep client.js , worker.js , and host.js together. For the custom totals view, copy views/.build/metric-totals.wasm and metric-totals.json into browser-demo/portable/ , then change the connection to: const db = await BrowserDatabase.connect({ name: 'metric-totals', base: new URL('./portable/', import.meta.url), }); The browser verifies the manifest's SHA-256 and descriptor before execution. db.info contains initial stats; await db.stats() exposes the current module digest, descriptor, checkpoints, document count, cursor, and Wasm memory size. Compare module_sha256 with Python's PortableView.sha256 to confirm the exact artifact. query({limit,cursor,after,key}) returns snapshot pages; continue with both returned cursor and after. rows({limit,key}) collects all pages into an array. changes(cursor,{limit}) returns one change page; continue with its returned cursor until complete. ingest(resolvedDocuments) replays exported records with their retained identities and positions. add(payload,{id,source,position}) accepts an optional explicit identity. export() returns all resolved records. replay() rebuilds with original committed batches and reports equivalence of keys, states, and results. The computation contract and limits Operation Input Output descriptor Module request Name, view version, state version, ABI, merge capability map A batch of document payloads An emission array per document, including zero emissions identity Empty request Initial JSON state for a group add State and ordered contributions Updated JSON state finalize State Public JSON result merge Two compatible states Combined state, when supported The v1 ABI uses UTF-8 JSON with a 256 KiB request limit and a separate 256 KiB response limit, both including envelopes. Modules have no host imports and at most 16 MiB of linear memory. The native host imposes a fuel budget. The browser client runs a dedicated worker with a 15-second default deadline, configurable through timeoutMs from 1 through 60,000 milliseconds. Expiry terminates the worker and loses its in-memory state. Both hosts limit an ingestion batch to 1024 documents and 4096 emissions, and snapshot pages to 1024 entries. Encoded map and per-group add requests can reach the ABI byte limit earlier. The browser additionally caps retained documents at 20,000 and 16 MiB of encoded records, distinct groups at 4096, and history at 100,000 entries and 32 MiB of encoded rows. Its public request envelope is capped at 4 MiB. These are component limits, not a bound on the whole browser process. A failing batch does not commit a prefix. Portable JSON numbers use IEEE-754 double precision, as in JavaScript. Python rejects integer inputs that cannot be represented exactly as doubles; use strings for exact large identifiers. Positions and cursor sequences are nonnegative JavaScript-safe integers. Floating-point sums preserve ordered inputs; arbitrary merge trees can change rounding. See numerical reproducibility . Retain documents; regenerate views Keep resolved documents and the exact compiled module outside derived storage. Reopen native storage with identical module bytes to reuse checkpoints; to change the module, open a fresh database and replay in original ingestion order. A matching human version label does not override a changed digest. with PortableDatabase("portable-rebuilt.db", view) as rebuilt: rebuilt.ingest(retained) assert list(rebuilt.rows())[0].result["mean"] == 5 For larger streams, iterate db.ingest_many(records, batch_size=100) ; each yielded result commits one bounded batch. db.documents(limit=100) exports resolved records at a pinned snapshot. Browser exports include an additional engine sequence field; Python accepts them after constructing Document objects: import json from pathlib import Path from foldlitedb import Document, PortableDatabase, PortableView view = PortableView.bundled("metrics") records = json.loads(Path("exported-documents.json").read_text(), parse_int=float) documents = [Document(r["id"], r["payload"], int(r["position"]), r["source"]) for r in records] with PortableDatabase("from-browser.db", view) as db: for result in db.ingest_many(documents): print(result.inserted, result.replayed) The final snippet expects an exported JSON array from the metrics view. Browser payload numbers use IEEE-754 doubles; parse_int=float preserves those semantics even when a large double is serialized without a decimal point. Safe source positions are converted back to Python integers when constructing documents. Preserve input order; preserve batch boundaries too if exact engine sequence values matter. Compare computation outputs rather than database-local cursors. A new database receives a new identity, so its cursors differ even when results match. Native storage persists across reopen; browser state is in memory and is discarded on reload or close() . Export before closing and ingest those records into a new worker to restore it. Persistent browser storage, portable history compaction, and multiple native views per database remain future extensions. The replay model explains how this differs from callback view rebuilds.

title: Python API
text: Reference · development API The Python API PortableDatabase runs a complete Wasm map/reduce view in Rust. The existing Database API runs Python callbacks. Both expose immutable documents, atomic batches, snapshots, and changes. PortableView and packaged assets PortableView(module, *, sha256=None) PortableView.bundled(name="metrics") → PortableView portable_assets() → importlib.resources Traversable Import these names from foldlitedb . module accepts Wasm bytes or a filesystem path. PortableView stores immutable module bytes and their sha256 ; an optional digest must match exactly. Module size is 1 byte through 16 MiB. Exports, imports, ABI, and descriptor are validated when the native database opens. bundled accepts "metrics" or "catalogue" and verifies the packaged manifest digest. Metrics returns {count,sum,min,max,mean} ; catalogue returns {count,items} after its ordered item fold. The portable guide describes accepted payloads. portable_assets() exposes both modules and manifests plus the buildless browser hosts. Copy its files using their resource read_bytes() methods; resources need not be ordinary filesystem paths. PortableDatabase PortableDatabase(path, view=None) A Rust/SQLite database executing one complete portable view. view accepts a PortableView , Wasm bytes, or a module path. Omit it to use the bundled metrics view. path accepts a filesystem path or ":memory:" . Parent directories must already exist. Use a context manager or close() . Closing is idempotent; later operations raise DatabaseError . Reopening the same file and exact module reuses persisted state. Different module bytes fail: create a new file and replay retained documents to upgrade. Cursors bind to a database identity and exact module digest. from foldlitedb import PortableDatabase, PortableView with PortableDatabase(":memory:", PortableView.bundled("metrics")) as portable: original = portable.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, id="a") assert portable.add(original.payload, id="a") == original snapshot = portable.query() portable.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 8}) assert portable.changes(since=snapshot.cursor).rows[0].result["mean"] == 6 retained = tuple(portable.documents()) assert portable.stats()["documents"] == 2 with PortableDatabase(":memory:") as replay: assert replay.ingest(retained).inserted == 2 assert replay.ingest(retained).replayed == 2 Append and replay db.add(payload, *, id=None, source="default", position=None) → Document db.add_many(payloads, *, source="default") → tuple[Document, ...] db.ingest(documents) → IngestResult db.ingest_many(documents, *, batch_size=100) → iterator[IngestResult] add appends one finite JSON payload and returns its resolved Document(id, payload, position, source) . Omitted IDs are generated; omitted positions start at zero and advance per source. An identical named add or replay at an existing source position reuses the original document. Conflicting reuse fails; previously unseen positions must advance that source's checkpoint. IDs and sources are nonempty strings of at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes. Positions range from zero through 2**53 - 1 . add_many eagerly consumes one iterable of payloads and commits atomically, returning resolved records in input order. Each member is one JSON payload, including an entire array. Empty input returns () ; retrying unnamed payloads appends new records. ingest instead requires Document instances with retained identities, positions, and payloads; its result contains inserted , replayed , and sequence . Identical replay skips map execution. ingest_many is lazy. Iterating commits separate batches of 1–1024 documents, defaulting to 100. A later error preserves previously committed batches. All atomic ingestion calls are limited to 1024 documents and 4096 map emissions. The complete map request, including its envelope and all newly inserted payloads, must fit 256 KiB; per-group add requests, states, and results must also fit their Wasm buffers. Reduce batch size for larger payloads. Map, reducer, validation, and limit errors roll back the whole current batch. Portable JSON uses IEEE-754 double precision and at most 64 nesting levels. Python rejects integer inputs that cannot be represented exactly as a double. Encode identifiers requiring arbitrary integer precision as strings. Nonfinite numbers and invalid Unicode scalar values fail before execution. Rows, snapshot pages, and changes db.rows(*, key=<omitted>, limit=100) → iterator[Row] db.query(*, key=<omitted>, limit=100, cursor=None, after=None) → Snapshot db.changes(*, since, limit=100) → ChangePage Portable reads omit a view name. rows lazily follows snapshot pages, pinning the committed prefix on first iteration. limit is a page size from 1 through 1024, not a total row limit. Omit key for every group or supply any JSON key, including null, for exact filtering. Rows follow canonical JSON lexical order consistent with the browser host. No transaction spans a yield to application code. A Row contains key , reducer state , finalized result , and committed sequence . A Snapshot contains rows , cursor , after , and complete . Continue with both returned cursor and after , keeping the same key filter. New documents do not change that snapshot. with PortableDatabase(":memory:") as portable: portable.add_many([ {"metric": "a", "value": 2}, {"metric": "b", "value": 8}, ]) page = portable.query(limit=1) snapshot_cursor = page.cursor rows = list(page.rows) while not page.complete: page = portable.query(limit=1, cursor=page.cursor, after=page.after) rows.extend(page.rows) assert [row.key for row in rows] == ["a", "b"] portable.add({"metric": "a", "value": 4}) changes = portable.changes(since=snapshot_cursor, limit=1) assert changes.rows[0].result["mean"] == 3 while not changes.complete: changes = portable.changes(since=changes.cursor, limit=1) changes reads committed group postimages after a snapshot or change cursor. Pass since=0 to read retained history from the start. A page contains rows , a continuation cursor , and complete ; continue with that cursor. Multiple updates to one key in a batch coalesce into one postimage. A page can split a batch's group updates. Zero-emission documents still advance progress. Cursors belong to their original database and cannot be transferred to a replayed database. Export and inspect db.documents(*, limit=100) → iterator[Document] db.stats() → dict db.close() documents exports resolved source records in original ingestion order at a fixed snapshot, pinned on first iteration. Its page size is 1–1024. Retain these records outside the derived cache and feed them to ingest or ingest_many for replay. stats returns documents (count), sequence , cursor , module_sha256 , descriptor , and checkpoints (source-to-position mapping). Engine sequence includes document and group-state records, so it is not a document count. Snapshot and sequence values can differ when replay uses different batch boundaries. The native engine uses SQLite WAL with full synchronous commits and a five-second busy timeout. Separate connections coordinate writes through SQLite; calls on a native engine are serialized. Retained documents and view history grow on disk. This API currently exposes no compaction, callback registration, reset, or in-place module rebuild. Choose a computation path Capability PortableDatabase Database Map input JSON payload inside Wasm Document in a Python callback View setup One module passed to the constructor One or more View registrations Read methods rows() , query() , changes(since=...) Same methods with a view name Changed computation New database plus replay Changed declared definition rebuilds its view Browser execution Same compiled map/reduce module Bundled numeric reducers only; Python callbacks stay in Python Runtime dependency Packaged native Rust extension Python SQLite; Wasmtime extra for numeric reducers Use separate files: the two APIs have different schemas and cursor formats. Neither API selects the other backend implicitly. The remaining reference describes the callback API. Database: Python callbacks Database(path, *, generation="default", reset=False, max_batch=1024, max_batch_bytes=8 * 1024 * 1024, max_value_bytes=1024 * 1024, max_key_bytes=4096, max_page_bytes=8 * 1024 * 1024, max_emissions_per_document=1024, timeout=30) A local SQLite view cache, safe to share between Python threads. Separate instances and processes serialize writes through SQLite. Use a context manager or call close() . generation identifies the source collection. A conflicting generation requires an explicit reset=True , which discards derived storage and invalidates existing instances and cursors. Retain authoritative documents before resetting. Limit Meaning max_batch Maximum documents in one atomic ingestion call. max_batch_bytes Encoded payload, document-ID, and source bytes per batch; also bounds pending map values. max_value_bytes Encoded payload, contribution, reducer-state, and finalized-result size. max_key_bytes Encoded canonical JSON key size; cannot exceed 4096. max_page_bytes Total key, state, and result bytes in a returned page. max_emissions_per_document Bounds map output for each document. timeout SQLite lock wait in finite seconds, from 0 to 2147483.647. Adding documents add db.add(payload, *, id=None, source="default", position=None) → Document Append any finite JSON value. Omitted IDs are generated; omitted positions start at zero or follow the source checkpoint. The returned payload is a separate JSON value, isolated from caller and mapper mutations. An identical named retry reuses its original position. A source and position can also identify an identical unnamed retry. Conflicting identity reuse raises DocumentConflict ; a new document behind its source checkpoint raises SourceOrderError . add_many db.add_many(payloads, *, source="default") → tuple[Document, ...] Eagerly consume one bounded iterable of JSON payloads and append it atomically. Every member is one payload, so an array is kept whole. Results preserve input order and have generated IDs and consecutive source positions. Empty input returns () . Input errors, map failures, limits, and position exhaustion roll back the entire batch. Retrying this unnamed call adds another batch. Replay retained documents with ingest . Explicit documents and batches Document(id, payload, position, source="default") db.ingest(documents) → IngestResult db.ingest_many(documents, *, batch_size=None) → iterator[IngestResult] ingest atomically commits a bounded batch of explicit Document records. Identical replay performs no map work and must match the ID, position, and payload. Its result has inserted , replayed , and the committed ingestion sequence . ingest_many is lazy: iteration commits separate bounded batches. The default batch size is max_batch ; a failure preserves previously committed batches. Views and reducers View(name, version, map, reducer, references={}) db.register(view) → revision A map receives a Document and yields zero or more (key, contribution) pairs. Keys and values may be structured finite JSON. Each key owns a reducer state. The view version identifies map behavior; references declares captured external-input versions. Register callbacks on every instance that reads their views. Registration reuses compatible persisted state or rebuilds a changed definition atomically. Query and change reads catch registered callbacks up after another connection ingests documents. Numeric reducers Mean(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) Sum(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) Count(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) Envelope(*, runtime=None, positioned=False) RustReducer(name, *, runtime=None, positioned=False) Install the callback numeric runtime from your checkout with python -m pip install '.[reducers]' . The source build requires Rust; installing a matching wheel does not. The named constructors use the same descriptors and state formats as their explicit reducer IDs. They load the optional runtime when computation needs it. Ordinary maps emit finite numbers or null; null contributes nothing. Constructor Reducer ID Result Mean() mean/v1 {"count": n, "value": mean} ; empty value is null. Sum() sum/v1 Count and sum; empty sum is zero. Count() count/v1 Count and count value; counts non-null numeric emissions. Envelope() envelope/v1 Count and first/min/max/last points, each with value and position. Map a document to 1 to count it. Envelope order uses source positions plus deterministic identity/emission tie breaking. positioned=True accepts explicitly positioned portable contributions; it is intended for adapters that already own that position schema. OrderedFold OrderedFold(initial, step, *, version, finalize=None) A trusted Python fold for structured state. step(state, contribution) returns the next finite JSON state. Steps run in persisted ingestion order within a key. Ordered folds do not declare arbitrary partial-state merging. from foldlitedb import Database, OrderedFold, View def statuses(document): yield document.payload["record"], document.payload["status"] status = View("status", "1", statuses, OrderedFold(None, lambda previous, value: value, version="1")) with Database(":memory:") as db: db.register(status) db.add_many([ {"record": "a", "status": "open"}, {"record": "a", "status": "closed"}, ]) assert list(db.rows("status"))[0].result == "closed" Rows, snapshots, and changes rows db.rows(name, *, key=<omitted>, limit=100) → iterator[Row] Lazily iterate a stable snapshot in bounded pages. The first iteration selects its committed prefix. limit controls page size, from 1 to 4096; it does not cap total results. No transaction or lock spans a yield to application code. Omit key for every group. Supplying any JSON key, including null, filters exactly. Keys follow canonical JSON lexical order. View rebuilds and compaction can expire a paused iterator. query db.query(name, *, key=<omitted>, limit=100, after=None, cursor=None) → Snapshot A snapshot contains rows , cursor , after , and complete . Continue pages with both the original cursor and the returned after . Each Row contains key , finalized result , reducer state , and ingestion sequence . changes db.changes(name, *, since, limit=100) → ChangePage Read committed key postimages after a snapshot or change cursor. A change page has rows , a continuation cursor , and complete . Continue using that page's cursor. Changes coalesce repeated updates to the same key within one transaction. A page can split a transaction; its cursor retains per-key progress. Empty maps still advance progress. Lookup and maintenance get(identifier, *, source="default") → Document | None Read a cached immutable document with a freshly decoded payload. checkpoint(source="default") → int | None Read the highest committed source position. refresh(name) Explicitly catch a registered view up to retained documents. Ordinary reads do this automatically. compact(name, *, before) Discard older change history while preserving the chosen snapshot boundary. The caller owns reader retention. stats() Return document, source, view, state, history counts and current ingestion sequence. Errors For the portable API, validation and Wasm failures raise DatabaseError ; conflicting replay, source ordering, and invalid cursors use DocumentConflict , SourceOrderError , and CursorExpired where identified. A missing native extension raises an actionable RuntimeError . DatabaseError extends ValueError . Its specialized errors are DocumentConflict , SourceOrderError , CursorExpired , and GenerationMismatch . Failing callbacks propagate their exceptions and roll back their transaction. Missing numeric runtime support raises an actionable RuntimeError .

title: Replay and ordering
text: The model Replay and ordering Documents are immutable observations. Views are the changing state derived from them. Stable identity, ordered inputs, and exact computation definitions make that state recoverable. Names are optional add(payload) assigns an internal ID. Equal unnamed payloads still represent separate observations. A caller-supplied name tells the host that an identical repeated call refers to one observation. An identical named retry skips mapping and keeps its original position, even after the source advances. Changing that name's payload is a conflict. Model a changing lifecycle by appending a new observation and folding its status. This identity model applies to the native portable host, the browser host, and the callback API. Positions track a source A position means “this document's offset in its source.” Automatic positions start at zero and follow that source's committed checkpoint. External logs can supply monotonically increasing offsets with gaps. from foldlitedb import PortableDatabase, SourceOrderError with PortableDatabase(":memory:") as db: first = db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, source="training.log", position=10) db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, source="training.log", position=40) assert db.add(first.payload, source="training.log", position=10) == first assert db.stats()["checkpoints"]["training.log"] == 40 try: db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}, source="training.log", position=30) except SourceOrderError: pass else: raise AssertionError("New records cannot arrive behind the checkpoint") IDs and positions are scoped to a source. An existing source position can identify a replay without a caller-supplied ID; payloads and any supplied ID must match. Previously unseen positions behind the checkpoint fail. Positions range from zero through 2**53 - 1 . Avoid mixing automatic positions with external offsets unless they share the same progression. Source checkpoints advance in the same transaction as documents and view states. Ingestion order is separate Ordered portable views, such as the bundled catalogue, and Python OrderedFold process contributions in ingestion order within a key. Source offsets do not sort records across sources; timestamps do not reorder an existing fold. Applications choose domain order before ingestion and replay that order. Portable maps receive document payloads only. Their host tracks IDs, source positions, deduplication, and ingestion order. Callback maps receive complete Document records and can inspect that metadata. Include needed domain metadata inside portable payloads. The callback API's numeric Envelope has a separate ordering contract: declared source position plus deterministic source/identity/emission tie breaking. It does not imply that the portable metrics module or all custom views use envelope ordering. Keep the source outside the cache Retain resolved documents and exact computation artifacts outside derived storage. Native documents() and browser export() expose retained records, but exporting a copy is the application's responsibility. from foldlitedb import PortableView view = PortableView.bundled("metrics") with PortableDatabase("live.db", view) as live: live.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) retained = tuple(live.documents()) expected = [(r.key, r.state, r.result) for r in live.rows()] with PortableDatabase("rebuilt.db", view) as rebuilt: rebuilt.ingest(retained) assert [(r.key, r.state, r.result) for r in rebuilt.rows()] == expected assert rebuilt.ingest(retained).replayed == 2 Keeping payloads alone and assigning new identities does not preserve the source replay contract. It can also change callback computations that inspect document identity or numeric envelope tie positions. A label for a lost taxonomy or reference snapshot cannot reproduce its contents. Portable add implementations must give equivalent results for the same ordered contributions split across successive batches. Preserve batch boundaries if exact engine sequence values matter: a sequence includes committed document and group-state records. Replayed databases have new identities and cursors even when their computed states match. Browser replay() retains the original batches and compares keys, states, and results. Module changes and callback versions Portable views: the SHA-256 digest identifies the complete compiled map, reducer, state schema, and SDK runtime. Native storage reopens only with the exact same bytes. Changed modules require a fresh database plus retained-document replay. Update the view version for changed behavior and the state version for incompatible formats; rebuild the manifest too. Matching labels do not override a different digest. Compiler changes can also alter the digest. Python callbacks: View.version identifies map behavior; the fold and reducer have their own versions, and references declares captured external inputs. Registering a compatible definition reuses checkpoints. A changed definition rebuilds that callback view atomically from retained documents and invalidates its old cursors. Changing a callable or captured input requires updating its declared definition. Python callbacks are trusted application code. Portable modules have no host imports and run with bounded memory and execution, but they must still be deterministic: use explicit inputs and state rather than mutable global data. Hosts instantiate portable modules afresh for operations. Neither path automatically makes arbitrary state mergeable. Native persistence and browser memory PortableDatabase uses the Rust engine's SQLite WAL storage. Documents, source checkpoints, states, and history survive a close and reopen. Different native connections coordinate writes through SQLite. The callback API uses a separate Python/SQLite schema; its files and cursors are not interchangeable with portable storage. The browser host executes the same Wasm computation, while JavaScript retains documents, grouped states, and history in a dedicated worker. It currently uses no IndexedDB or persistent browser database. Reloading the page, closing the client, or a worker deadline discards state. Export resolved records before closing, then ingest them into a new worker to restore the view. Native storage grows with retained documents, keys, and history. The browser preview instead rejects batches that exceed its document, key, history, and byte limits; see exact component limits . A 16 MiB Wasm linear-memory limit is not a limit on the entire host process. Atomic commits and stable reads A batch commits identities, checkpoints, reduced states, and change records together. A validation, map, reducer, or limit error rolls back the whole current batch. ingest_many commits separate batches as you iterate; earlier successful batches survive a later error. A snapshot cursor identifies a database, computation revision, and committed prefix. Snapshot pages retain that prefix while new documents arrive. Continue a query with both its cursor and after token, then use the snapshot cursor for later changes. Changes carry complete resulting key states, coalesced per key within each batch. Portable cursors belong to their original database identity and module. Native connections and reopens of the same file with the same module can reuse cursors; a new browser worker or rebuilt database has a new identity and cannot reuse them. Row iterators release transactions between pages. The portable API currently retains all history and exposes no compaction. Callback Database.compact can discard old changes at an explicit caller-selected boundary, expiring older readers while retaining documents for rebuilds. Numerical reproducibility Portable payloads, keys, states, and results use finite IEEE-754 doubles, matching JavaScript numbers. Python rejects integer inputs that cannot be represented exactly as a double. Large exactly representable values still use double semantics; encode arbitrary-precision identifiers as strings. Positions and engine sequences must remain in the nonnegative JavaScript-safe integer range. JSON nesting is bounded to 64 levels. The same compiled AssemblyScript module runs in both native and browser portable hosts, using shared canonical key representation. Neither host adds Python arbitrary-precision arithmetic. Floating-point addition is not associative: arbitrary merge trees can change sum or mean rounding. Preserve input order and the declared partition/merge plan when exact agreement matters. Merge compatible states with disjoint coverage, rather than finalized means. The callback API's bundled numeric reducers are a separate Rust mathematical kernel compiled to Wasm. Its count and envelope have exact merge contracts within their input bounds; sum and mean have floating-point merge limits. That reducer-only ABI is distinct from the complete AssemblyScript view ABI. A bundled module change can affect each API's cached-state identity through its respective upgrade rules.

title: Native experiments
text: Engineering notes Native experiments Experimental Historical measurements compare Python callback views with a separate native numeric field-map prototype. These reports describe those implementations, not the newer portable-view engine. The callback baseline and newer portable path The measured callback Database baseline uses Python SQLite for document identity, ordered retention, state, history, and checkpoints. Trusted Python maps and ordered folds run in Python; bundled numeric reducers run the shared Rust core through WebAssembly. The newer portable engine runs complete AssemblyScript maps and reducers through Rust and exposes PortableDatabase . It is separate from both this callback baseline and the field-projection experiment below. These historical throughput results do not benchmark that new engine. Neither Python API silently switches backends. A deliberately limited prototype The experimental engine runs native Rust with optional Python bindings, using the same reducer core across SQLite and a durable custom log. Its view contract is a single declarative numeric view over top-level fields, rather than arbitrary Python maps or ordered folds. Separate experiment. Backend compatibility, durability, worker ordering, and numerical behavior need explicit verification. Prototype throughput is not a performance promise for the full Python database API. To reproduce the experiment, install this checkout with the callback numeric extra, then build the experimental package separately. Both source builds require Rust and a platform C toolchain. Installing a matching prebuilt main-package wheel needs no compiler; this development API has not been released on PyPI. python -m pip install '.[reducers]' python -m pip install ./experimental/python from foldlitedb_experimental import NativeDatabase, NativeView metrics = NativeView("metrics", "metric", "value", reducer="mean/v1") with NativeDatabase("native.log", metrics, backend="log", workers=4) as db: retained = db.add_many([ {"metric": "loss", "value": 4}, {"metric": "loss", "value": 8}, ]) assert list(db.rows())[0].result == {"count": 2, "value": 6.0} with NativeDatabase("native.log", metrics, backend="log", workers=4) as db: assert db.ingest(retained).replayed == 2 snapshot = db.query() db.add({"metric": "loss", "value": 3}) assert db.changes(since=snapshot.cursor).rows[0].result == { "count": 3, "value": 5.0, } Choose backend="sqlite" for the experimental SQLite journal. The native query methods omit a view name because a database has one view. NativeView also accepts a version, synthetic map-work amount, and emission count for controlled experiments. Current limits Only numeric field projections and the mean, sum, count, and envelope reducers are supported. Python callbacks, ordered folds, multiple views, in-place view rebuilds, and compaction are outside this prototype. Rust document mapping and emission use 1–64 workers. Grouping and per-key reduction currently run serially and preserve contribution order. The default worker count follows available CPUs, capped at 64. The expanded batch of emissions is buffered before reduction. Up to 1024 documents with 1024 emissions each can require substantial memory; streaming backpressure and compact worker shards are not implemented. Both backends append commit records and maintain in-memory indexes. Reopening replays the full journal; memory and retained history grow with data. Both backends hold an exclusive process lock. The callback database instead supports concurrent readers through SQLite. The experimental SQLite backend uses a journal-plus-memory layout, so storage comparisons do not isolate SQLite library overhead from all data-layout differences. Float-valued grouping keys, including floats nested in structured keys, use deterministic Rust JSON ordering that can differ from Python canonical JSON ordering because exponent formatting differs. Grouping and exact lookup still work; universal cross-engine row-order parity is not promised. Measured worker scaling Local medians from 156 fresh-process trials, with 2 repeats per configuration. The illustrated uniform workload has 4,096 documents, 128 keys, 512-document durable batches, and 8 live updates using mean/v1 . The host exposes 24 logical CPUs; storage is ext4 / /dev/mapper/nvme4tb . Ingestion timings exclude numeric runtime warm-up and include the same batch boundaries and durable acknowledgments. Within each matched workload, fixture and result hashes agree across engines and worker counts. Cheap field mapping Workers Native SQLite docs/s vs. 1 worker Native log docs/s vs. 1 worker 1 71,582 1.00× 72,002 1.00× 2 72,838 1.02× 74,964 1.04× 4 70,102 0.98× 73,277 1.02× 8 73,162 1.02× 73,858 1.03× 12 76,799 1.07× 75,263 1.05× 24 68,904 0.96× 75,437 1.05× Synthetic CPU-heavy mapping The artificial map performs 10,000 integer-mixing rounds per document. This measures available map parallelism, not an application speed guarantee. Workers Native SQLite docs/s vs. 1 worker Native log docs/s vs. 1 worker 1 33,543 1.00× 32,192 1.00× 2 44,420 1.32× 46,593 1.45× 4 54,858 1.64× 57,267 1.78× 8 62,924 1.88× 66,470 2.06× 12 66,808 1.99× 68,871 2.14× 24 67,607 2.02× 67,426 2.09× Cheap maps show no consistent multicore benefit. The synthetic case improves end-to-end ingestion by roughly two times, while its map phase scales further. Serial grouping, reduction, serialization, and commit costs remain. SQLite and the custom log are close in this fixture; neither is a categorical winner. Startup and memory remain part of the cost These one-worker rows use the cheap uniform workload. Setup includes explicit numeric runtime warm-up plus database opening; whole-process peak memory includes the Python host. The native backends replay their full journal on reopening. Engine Setup + warm-up Reopen + full query Peak RSS Storage Python / SQLite + WASM 67.22 ms 13.36 ms 82.2 MiB 668 KiB Native / SQLite 5.67 ms 8.37 ms 37.3 MiB 552 KiB Native / log 1.37 ms 9.45 ms 34.8 MiB 534 KiB No OS page-cache eviction was performed. These small, two-repeat measurements do not establish large-history reopen cost, bounded memory, or production latency. The Python/native comparison also changes data layout and algorithms; worker-count comparisons within one native backend isolate parallelism more closely. Download the complete NVMe/ext4 report for every distribution, individual sample, latency, phase cost, and source hash. The separate tmpfs run is supplementary CPU-oriented evidence and is not used in these storage tables. Payload size probe A separate 30-trial NVMe/ext4 probe adds unused ASCII padding of 0, 1 KiB, or 16 KiB per document while preserving numeric map results. Each configuration uses 512 documents plus 8 live records, 64-document durable batches, 128 keys, and two repeats. Compare sizes within this probe; its batch size differs from the worker-scaling matrix. Padding / document Python SQLite docs/s Native SQLite, 1 worker Native SQLite, 4 workers Native log, 1 worker Native log, 4 workers 0 B 5,031 38,219 39,102 41,660 40,202 1 KiB 4,736 26,932 29,268 31,304 32,499 16 KiB 3,296 4,884 4,883 6,324 6,936 Actual encoded fixture sizes, including identities and live records, are 47,880, 587,120, 8,574,320 bytes respectively. At 16 KiB padding, median whole-process peak RSS for one worker is Python: 97.9 MiB, native SQLite: 58.6 MiB, native log: 54.9 MiB. Larger ignored payloads exercise JSON serialization, validation, copying, retained storage, and durability together; these timings do not isolate one cause. Peak RSS also includes fixture objects, encoded input, and the Python host. This small padding probe does not establish behavior for every nested document shape or high-fanout map. Download the complete payload probe . The original 156-trial results remain unchanged, with their measured runner hash and source commit preserved in the primary report; the new padding option is additive and defaults to zero. Measure complete workloads The existing deterministic benchmark measures document construction, mapping, numeric reduction, transactions, queries, reopening, and regeneration: mkdir -p .benchmark-storage python scripts/benchmark_database.py \ --documents 100000 --keys 128 --batch-size 1024 \ --live-documents 100 --storage-root .benchmark-storage \ --output /tmp/foldlite-database.json Its initial ingestion includes lazy runtime compilation. Live operations reuse that instance; same-process reopening and regeneration reuse the compiled module but create fresh instances. Its “rebuild” timing means registering before ingestion, not rebuilding a view over an already retained history. Compare native and WASM execution with storage held constant, then compare storage with computation held constant. Report startup separately from warmed operation and match the durable acknowledgment boundary. Choose the filesystem you mean to measure explicitly: temporary directories can be backed by memory. Keep tmpfs results separate from measurements on a persistent storage device. The comparison matrix Dimension Cases to distinguish Data Low/high key cardinality; uniform, hot-key, and clustered distributions; small and nested payloads. Computation Count, envelope, sum, mean; cheap/expensive maps; zero, one, and many emissions. Execution Batch sizes; worker counts; native/WASM boundaries; queue and merge costs. Storage Durable SQLite and custom log with equivalent acknowledgment semantics; memory-only results reported separately. Lifecycle Historical registration, live reads, change feeds, restart, suffix catch-up, and regeneration. Evidence Throughput, latency distributions, total process memory, disk/log size, runtime versions, fixture hash, and numerical agreement. Correctness before speedups Out-of-order worker completion must preserve document and emission order where required. Duplicate, overlapping, missing, and retried worker ranges must not double-count or advance progress past unfinished work. Failure, cancellation, process exit, and torn writes must preserve the promised commit boundary. Snapshot pages and change feeds must expose committed prefixes and retain explicit cursor expiry. Count and envelope require exact agreement; sum and mean need a declared numerical contract and deterministic merge plan. Slow tasks and high-cardinality keys must not create unbounded queues or memory growth. Parallel key reduction and parallel mapping are different capabilities. Python ordered folds cannot use arbitrary partial-state merging. Any future fast path must state the semantics it supports.
